title: What Will Post-Training Fix? Per-Problem Gains Are Shared Across Independent RL Runs,and Existing Checkpoints Predict Them Better Than A Priori Signals

paper.title: What Will Post-Training Fix? Per-Problem Gains Are Shared Across Independent RL Runs, and Existing Checkpoints Predict Them Better Than A Priori Signals
paper.abstract: Abstract Data selection, curricula and the evaluation of post-training recipes all assume that we can tell, before training, which problems a model will improve on. We test this assumption directly. For two base models, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, we evaluate eighteen post-training runs on up to 1532 competition math problems with many samples per problem, and compare signals available before training against a noise ceiling derived from the agreement between disjoint subsets of runs. Three findings hold on both base models. What post-training fixes is shared: independent runs agree on which rarely solved problems improve, with a noise ceiling of about 0.9 0.9 , yet the two base models agree with each other only at ρ = 0.25 \rho=0.25 —the shared component belongs to the base model, not to the problem. A priori signals capture a minority of it: base pass rate, the likelihood of a correct solution, a larger model’s pass rate and their combinations explain only 0.30 0.30 and 0.24 0.24 of the explainable variance in gains. Existing checkpoints are the better predictor: the per-problem gains of a single checkpoint from another family predict a new run better than every a priori signal, alone or combined ( 0.52 0.52 vs. 0.33 0.33 and 0.34 0.34 vs. 0.17 0.17 against the combined signals). The conclusions hold on problems from 2025–2026 competitions and when the baselines on the two sides of every comparison are estimated independently. We propose the noise ceiling as a standard companion to per-problem signals.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Post-training with verifiable rewards has become the main lever for improving reasoning in language models [ 8 , 24 , 33 ] , and with it a set of per-problem decisions has become routine. Pipelines discard problems whose rollouts are all wrong; curricula order problems by the model’s current pass rate; recent methods route on pass rate and then keep the verified solutions the model finds most likely [ 30 ] ; and practitioners compare recipes by which held-out problems they improve. Each of these decisions presumes an answer to a basic question: before post-training, can we tell which problems a model will improve on? A common intuition is a notion we call closeness . A model is expected to gain on problems it is already near to solving, as measured by its pass rate or by the likelihood it assigns to a correct solution. Closeness is intuitive and cheap, but it has rarely been evaluated against a yardstick that separates a weak signal from an unpredictable target. Whether a run improves a problem depends on the run’s data, algorithm and seed and on finite evaluation, so a weak predictor and an unpredictable target look the same. And most studies observe one run, so what is shared across recipes cannot be separated from what is specific to one. We resolve both difficulties with a simple design and evaluate closeness against the right yardstick. Holding the base model fixed, we collect many post-training runs released by different groups and evaluate each of them, with many samples per problem, on the same held-out problems. Agreement between disjoint subsets of runs gives a noise ceiling : the highest correlation any signal can be expected to reach with the runs’ consensus. A signal can then be judged by the fraction of the explainable variance it captures, rather than by a raw correlation of unknown meaning. We carry out this design on two base models with different post-training histories, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (eight runs) and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (ten runs), and report only conclusions that hold on both. sections.heading: Findings.
sections.text: 1. What post-training fixes is shared across independent runs. Runs from different groups and with different algorithms agree on which rarely solved problems improve. The noise ceiling for their consensus is about 0.9 0.9 on both base models, the agreement holds on recent competition problems, and it is specific to the base model: gains on the two bases correlate at only 0.25 0.25 (Section 4 ). 2. A priori signals capture a minority of the shared component. The strongest single signal on each base reaches about half the ceiling, and the best single signal or cross-validated combination explains 0.30 0.30 and 0.24 0.24 of the explainable variance in gains (Figure 1 , Section 5 ). The missing part lives in the base model’s behaviour on a problem, not in what the problem looks like. 3. Existing checkpoints are the better predictor. A single checkpoint from another family predicts which problems a new run will improve better than the best base-model signal for 17 of 18 held-out runs, and better than a larger model’s pass rate for 16 of 18 (Section 6 ). Together these results change how per-problem prediction in post-training should be thought of. What a run will fix is not noise: it is a stable property of the base model and the problem, reproduced by runs from different groups and algorithms and distinct from one base model to the next. Yet the closeness statistics on which data selection and curricula are built see only a minority of it, while the outcomes of runs that already exist see much more. The gap between the two is now measurable, and closing it is a concrete target for the next generation of selection methods.

sections.heading: Base models and runs.
sections.text: Base A is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B [ 8 ] . Its eight runs are six public RLVR checkpoints from six groups—JustRL [ 11 ] , DeepScaleR [ 19 ] , ProRL [ 17 ] , STILL-3 [ 21 ] , Open-RS3 [ 7 ] and FastCuRL [ 25 ] —and two on-policy distillation (OPD) runs that we train from JustRL following Fu et al. [9] . Our full-data OPD run reproduces the reported result (69.5 vs. 69.8 macro accuracy on MATH-500/AMC23/AIME25). Base B is Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B [ 31 ] . Its ten runs are public RL checkpoints from eight groups, including Oat-Zero [ 18 ] , three One-Shot RLVR checkpoints [ 28 ] , ExGRPO [ 36 ] , ReLIFT [ 20 ] and a spurious-rewards checkpoint [ 23 ] ; the full list is in Appendix A . We call runs that share a lineage a family : JustRL and the two OPD runs distilled from it on Base A, and the three One-Shot checkpoints on Base B. Independent runs come from different families: on Base B we keep one checkpoint per family (eight runs); on Base A we drop the JustRL family entirely, because our OPD runs inherit their teacher’s behaviour (five runs).

sections.heading: Problems.
sections.text: We pool MATH-500 [ 13 ] , AMC23, AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, OlympiadBench [ 12 ] and a subset of Omni-MATH [ 10 ] , and remove every problem whose normalised statement matches a problem in DAPO-17k or in five public RL training sets used by the Base A runs, leaving 1264 problems. We add 268 problems from 2025–2026 competitions collected by MathArena [ 1 ] , which are newer than the training data of the Base A checkpoints; we analyse them separately, as a held-out check, and for each base model use those it rarely solves; Base B is evaluated on all 1532 problems.

sections.heading: Sampling and outcomes.
sections.text: Base A models generate up to 31,744 tokens and Base B models up to 3,072 tokens (the context limit of Qwen2.5-Math), with temperature 0.7 and top- p p 0.9; all outputs are graded by the same rule-based verifier. Each base model is sampled 256 times per problem (64 times for one batch of Base A problems, Appendix A ) and each post-trained model 64 times. We study problems the base model rarely solves, with base pass rate in ( 0 , 25 / 256 ] (0,25/256] , and take as outcome the gain in pass rate from base to post-trained model. On Base B, part of the gain on many problems comes from the base model failing to finish with a final boxed answer, which RL training corrects: the fraction of base samples without a final answer correlates with gain at ρ = 0.26 \rho=0.26 . Because this reflects answer formatting rather than the problem, our main analysis on Base B uses the 249 problems on which at most a quarter of base samples lack a final answer; results on all 395 problems are reported in Appendix B . The main analysis covers 156 problems on Base A and 249 on Base B.

sections.heading: A priori signals.
sections.text: Base pass rate comes from the base samples. Likelihood statistics need a correct solution that the base model did not write: we sample a larger model from the same family (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B for Base A, Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct for Base B) 64 times per problem, keep up to four correct solutions, and teacher-force the base model on them. From token log-probabilities ℓ t \ell_{t} and ranks r t r_{t} we compute the mean likelihood (the mean of ℓ t \ell_{t} over the central 90% of tokens, a symmetric variant of the trimmed statistic Xu et al. [30] use to rank verified solutions), the sequence log-probability ∑ t ℓ t \sum_{t}\ell_{t} , the worst-step log-probability min t ⁡ ℓ t \min_{t}\ell_{t} , the number of steps with r t > 16 r_{t}>16 , and the solution length. The larger-model pass rate is the 7B model’s own accuracy. Likelihood statistics are available on the 127 (Base A) and 191 (Base B) problems for which the larger model found a correct solution.

sections.heading: 3 A noise ceiling for per-problem prediction
sections.text: Let y p , j y_{p,j} be the gain of run j j on problem p p and y ¯ p \bar{y}_{p} its mean over a set of runs. For every split of the runs into two equal halves we compute the Spearman correlation between the half means across problems and average, obtaining the split-half agreement r r ; with an odd number of runs we leave one run out of each split. The Spearman–Brown formula [ 26 , 2 ] extends r r to the reliability R R of the mean over all runs; intuitively, it answers how reliable the average of all runs is, given how well two halves of them agree. Under the classical model in which each run’s outcome is a shared component plus run-specific deviation, no a priori predictor can be expected to correlate with y ¯ p \bar{y}_{p} more than R \sqrt{R} , which we call the noise ceiling; the construction is standard in neuroscience [ 22 ] and has been used to bound per-item predictability for language models [ 38 ] . A signal with correlation ρ \rho captures a fraction ρ 2 / R \rho^{2}/R of the explainable variance. Pearson correlations give the same ceilings ( 0.89 0.89 and 0.92 0.92 ). We complement the ceiling with a variance decomposition of single-run gains, in which the shared problem effect is the average covariance between different runs and sampling noise is the binomial variance of a 64-sample estimate. All intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals over problems.

sections.heading: Independent baselines.
sections.text: Every run’s gain subtracts the same estimate of the base pass rate. To make the comparison between runs fully independent, we also estimate it separately for the two sides of each comparison. On Base B we split the 256 base samples into 128 to select problems and compute base-model signals and two sets of 64 that serve as the two baselines, averaging over ten random splits; on Base A we draw 64 additional base samples per problem with a new seed and use them as the baseline for one side. We also report post-training accuracy as an outcome, which subtracts nothing.

The mean gain over independent runs has a noise ceiling of 0.89 0.89 on Base A and 0.90 0.90 on Base B. sections.heading: The shared component belongs to the base model.
sections.text: Both bases were evaluated on the same original pool, so we can ask whether the problems one base model improves on are the problems the other improves on. On the 152 problems that both bases solve at a rate in ( 0 , 0.5 ] (0,0.5] , the runs of each base agree strongly among themselves (ceilings 0.90 0.90 and 0.91 0.91 on exactly these problems), yet the mean gain on Base A and the mean gain on Base B correlate at only ρ = 0.25 \rho=0.25 [ 0.09 0.09 , 0.42 0.42 ]. What post-training fixes is a property of the base model’s relation to the problem: it is reproducible within a base model and largely distinct across base models.

sections.heading: It is independent of training-data overlap and of problem type.
sections.text: On Base A, the maximum character n-gram TF-IDF similarity between a problem and the union of public RL training sets is unrelated to its gain ( ρ = 0.04 \rho=0.04 ), and after removing the quarter of problems most similar to any training problem, the remaining problems retain an eight-run ceiling of 0.94 0.94 . An LLM annotated each problem three times, blind to outcomes, for topic, answer type, number of solution steps, case analysis, computational load, need for a key insight, need for a construction and answer-format ambiguity (three-way agreement 0.70 0.70 – 0.91 0.91 ); a model trained on all labels captures 0.02 0.02 of the explainable variance. The shared component is carried by the base model’s behaviour on the problem, not by what the problem looks like.

sections.heading: Gain versus accuracy.
sections.text: Gain is the outcome that matters for deciding where training helps, but signals are often evaluated against post-training accuracy instead. Accuracy is easier to predict, because it inherits the base model’s ability: the signals capture 0.54 0.54 and 0.58 0.58 of the explainable variance in accuracy, roughly twice the fraction for gains. Predicting where a model will end up is thus considerably easier than predicting how far it will move, and conclusions drawn from accuracy overstate how well a signal anticipates the effect of training.

Each run is held out in turn; we correlate its per-problem gains with those of one checkpoint from another family (averaged over such checkpoints), with the best base-model signal, and with the larger model’s pass rate. The base-model signal is selected on the mean of the remaining runs, so the held-out run never influences the choice. Problems with a reference solution: 127 on Base A, 191 on Base B. If what post-training fixes is shared across runs, then the runs that already exist should tell us what a new run will fix. We test this directly. Each run is held out in turn, and we ask how well its per-problem gains are predicted by three sources: a single checkpoint from another family, the best signal computable from the base model, and the larger model’s pass rate (Figure 2 ). To keep the comparison fair, the base-model signal is chosen on the remaining runs rather than on the held-out one. On both base models a single checkpoint from another family is the best predictor. It exceeds the best base-model signal by 0.16 0.16 [ 0.06 0.06 , 0.27 0.27 ] on Base A and 0.17 0.17 [ 0.07 0.07 , 0.23 0.23 ] on Base B, and wins for 8 8 of 8 8 and 9 9 of 10 10 held-out runs. It also beats the larger model’s pass rate by 0.13 0.13 and 0.12 0.12 , with intervals excluding zero, and a ridge model that combines all a priori signals and is fitted with ten-fold cross-validation to each held-out run’s own gains ( 0.33 0.33 and 0.17 0.17 ; the checkpoint wins for 8 of 8 and 9 of 10 held-out runs). Across individual pairs of checkpoints from different families the median correlation is 0.50 0.50 and 0.33 0.33 , and the best-matched pairs reach 0.74 0.74 and 0.68 0.68 . On Base A, prediction improves further as more checkpoints are pooled (Appendix B ; that analysis draws runs from any family). This result is the predictive face of the shared component of Section 4 : a single run’s gains contain the shared component plus run-specific variation, so they act as an achievable lower bound on the ceiling that requires no model of what the shared component is.

sections.heading: Independent baselines.
sections.text: With disjoint base samples for the checkpoint and the held-out run, the checkpoint reaches 0.37 0.37 on Base A, against 0.28 0.28 for the best base-model signal and 0.28 0.28 for the larger model, and 0.28 0.28 on Base B, against 0.16 0.16 and 0.21 0.21 . With post-training accuracy as outcome, a checkpoint from another family exceeds the larger model’s pass rate by 0.08 0.08 on Base A and 0.19 0.19 [ 0.12 0.12 , 0.29 0.29 ] on Base B.

sections.heading: A practical recipe.
sections.text: To anticipate which held-out problems a new post-training run of a base model will improve, evaluate the base model and one existing checkpoint of it with a few dozen samples per problem, and rank problems by the checkpoint’s gain. No reference solutions, larger models or likelihood computations are needed, and the ranking is more informative than any a priori statistic we tested. For base models that are being post-trained for the first time, the noise ceiling shows how much room is left for a priori signals to grow into.

sections.heading: Does post-training create new capabilities?
sections.text: Comparisons at large sampling budgets find that RLVR mostly sharpens capabilities the base model already has [ 35 ] , with analogous conclusions for on-policy distillation [ 27 , 14 ] ; others report expansion under prolonged training [ 17 ] , relate apparent limits to the composition of primitive skills [ 29 , 37 ] , or show that even spurious rewards improve Qwen2.5-Math [ 23 ] . We ask a different question: not whether the boundary moves in aggregate, but which problems move, and how predictable that is.

sections.heading: Per-problem outcomes of RLVR.
sections.text: Yang et al. [32] show, for public RLVR pairs, that problems with the same base success rate can have different post-RL success rates and that these differences repeat across independent generation halves of the same pair. We ask a complementary question: whether different runs on the same base model agree with each other on which problems improve, how much of that agreement any signal could predict, and whether it carries over to a different base model. Chakma et al. [3] show that difficulty labels estimated from few rollouts are unstable, which motivates our many-sample design. Chen et al. [4] identify training problems that remain unlearnable and observe that correct-rollout likelihoods are similarly distributed for learnable and unlearnable groups. Zhou et al. [39] estimate a learnability prior for training problems from short probe training under one recipe. Our signals require no training, our outcomes are on held-out problems, and our ceiling is defined across recipes and groups.

sections.heading: Selecting and allocating problems.
sections.text: Proposed signals include the student’s likelihood of verified solutions [ 30 ] , observed success counts [ 34 ] , internal circuit activations [ 5 ] and prefix recoverability [ 15 ] ; teacher-guided curricula [ 40 ] and strategy-conditioned exploration [ 6 ] target problems that are currently unsolvable. A recent controlled comparison finds no rollout-selection method that reliably beats uniform sampling [ 16 ] . Our measurements point to one reason: the closeness signals these methods build on capture only a minority of what post-training predictably changes. Reporting the noise ceiling alongside a signal’s correlation would make the remaining headroom explicit.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: Before post-training a model, can we tell which problems it will improve on? Across two base models and eighteen runs, the answer has three parts. What post-training fixes is shared across independent runs and specific to the base model. The closeness signals behind today’s data selection and curricula capture only a minority of it. And the outcomes of a single existing checkpoint capture more than any a priori signal, alone or combined. The noise ceiling turns the remaining gap into a number. We hope it becomes a routine companion to per-problem signals, and that closing the gap becomes a goal for the next generation of selection methods.

Per-Problem Gains Are Shared Across Independent RL Runs, and Existing Checkpoints Predict Them Better Than A Priori Signals Xiaoxian Duan Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: Zhongguancun Academy, Beijing, China Affiliation: Z.ai Email: duanxiaoxian2026@ia.ac.cn Abstract Data selection, curricula and the evaluation of post-training recipes all assume that we can tell, before training, which problems a model will improve on. We test this assumption directly. For two base models, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, we evaluate eighteen post-training runs on up to 1532 competition math problems with many samples per problem, and compare signals available before training against a noise ceiling derived from the agreement between disjoint subsets of runs. Three findings hold on both base models. What post-training fixes is shared: independent runs agree on which rarely solved problems improve, with a noise ceiling of about 0.9 0.9 , yet the two base models agree with each other only at ρ = 0.25 \rho=0.25 —the shared component belongs to the base model, not to the problem. A priori signals capture a minority of it: base pass rate, the likelihood of a correct solution, a larger model’s pass rate and their combinations explain only 0.30 0.30 and 0.24 0.24 of the explainable variance in gains. Existing checkpoints are the better predictor: the per-problem gains of a single checkpoint from another family predict a new run better than every a priori signal, alone or combined ( 0.52 0.52 vs. 0.33 0.33 and 0.34 0.34 vs. 0.17 0.17 against the combined signals). The conclusions hold on problems from 2025–2026 competitions and when the baselines on the two sides of every comparison are estimated independently. We propose the noise ceiling as a standard companion to per-problem signals. 1 Introduction Post-training with verifiable rewards has become the main lever for improving reasoning in language models [ 8 , 24 , 33 ] , and with it a set of per-problem decisions has become routine. Pipelines discard problems whose rollouts are all wrong; curricula order problems by the model’s current pass rate; recent methods route on pass rate and then keep the verified solutions the model finds most likely [ 30 ] ; and practitioners compare recipes by which held-out problems they improve. Each of these decisions presumes an answer to a basic question: before post-training, can we tell which problems a model will improve on? A common intuition is a notion we call closeness . A model is expected to gain on problems it is already near to solving, as measured by its pass rate or by the likelihood it assigns to a correct solution. Closeness is intuitive and cheap, but it has rarely been evaluated against a yardstick that separates a weak signal from an unpredictable target. Whether a run improves a problem depends on the run’s data, algorithm and seed and on finite evaluation, so a weak predictor and an unpredictable target look the same. And most studies observe one run, so what is shared across recipes cannot be separated from what is specific to one. We resolve both difficulties with a simple design and evaluate closeness against the right yardstick. Holding the base model fixed, we collect many post-training runs released by different groups and evaluate each of them, with many samples per problem, on the same held-out problems. Agreement between disjoint subsets of runs gives a noise ceiling : the highest correlation any signal can be expected to reach with the runs’ consensus. A signal can then be judged by the fraction of the explainable variance it captures, rather than by a raw correlation of unknown meaning. We carry out this design on two base models with different post-training histories, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (eight runs) and Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (ten runs), and report only conclusions that hold on both. Figure 1: A priori signals reach a minority of what is predictable, on both base models. All bars use the 127 (Base A) and 191 (Base B) rarely solved problems with a reference solution. “Few low-rank”: fewer reference-solution steps outside the base model’s top-16. Bars: Spearman correlation between each a priori signal and the mean per-problem gain of the runs on problems the base model rarely solves, with 95% bootstrap intervals; blue bars combine all signals with ten-fold cross-validation. Red line: noise ceiling on the same problems. Each signal is named in the direction associated with larger gains. Findings. 1. What post-training fixes is shared across independent runs. Runs from different groups and with different algorithms agree on which rarely solved problems improve. The noise ceiling for their consensus is about 0.9 0.9 on both base models, the agreement holds on recent competition problems, and it is specific to the base model: gains on the two bases correlate at only 0.25 0.25 (Section 4 ). 2. A priori signals capture a minority of the shared component. The strongest single signal on each base reaches about half the ceiling, and the best single signal or cross-validated combination explains 0.30 0.30 and 0.24 0.24 of the explainable variance in gains (Figure 1 , Section 5 ). The missing part lives in the base model’s behaviour on a problem, not in what the problem looks like. 3. Existing checkpoints are the better predictor. A single checkpoint from another family predicts which problems a new run will improve better than the best base-model signal for 17 of 18 held-out runs, and better than a larger model’s pass rate for 16 of 18 (Section 6 ). Together these results change how per-problem prediction in post-training should be thought of. What a run will fix is not noise: it is a stable property of the base model and the problem, reproduced by runs from different groups and algorithms and distinct from one base model to the next. Yet the closeness statistics on which data selection and curricula are built see only a minority of it, while the outcomes of runs that already exist see much more. The gap between the two is now measurable, and closing it is a concrete target for the next generation of selection methods. 2 Setup Base models and runs. Base A is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B [ 8 ] . Its eight runs are six public RLVR checkpoints from six groups—JustRL [ 11 ] , DeepScaleR [ 19 ] , ProRL [ 17 ] , STILL-3 [ 21 ] , Open-RS3 [ 7 ] and FastCuRL [ 25 ] —and two on-policy distillation (OPD) runs that we train from JustRL following Fu et al. [9] . Our full-data OPD run reproduces the reported result (69.5 vs. 69.8 macro accuracy on MATH-500/AMC23/AIME25). Base B is Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B [ 31 ] . Its ten runs are public RL checkpoints from eight groups, including Oat-Zero [ 18 ] , three One-Shot RLVR checkpoints [ 28 ] , ExGRPO [ 36 ] , ReLIFT [ 20 ] and a spurious-rewards checkpoint [ 23 ] ; the full list is in Appendix A . We call runs that share a lineage a family : JustRL and the two OPD runs distilled from it on Base A, and the three One-Shot checkpoints on Base B. Independent runs come from different families: on Base B we keep one checkpoint per family (eight runs); on Base A we drop the JustRL family entirely, because our OPD runs inherit their teacher’s behaviour (five runs). Problems. We pool MATH-500 [ 13 ] , AMC23, AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, OlympiadBench [ 12 ] and a subset of Omni-MATH [ 10 ] , and remove every problem whose normalised statement matches a problem in DAPO-17k or in five public RL training sets used by the Base A runs, leaving 1264 problems. We add 268 problems from 2025–2026 competitions collected by MathArena [ 1 ] , which are newer than the training data of the Base A checkpoints; we analyse them separately, as a held-out check, and for each base model use those it rarely solves; Base B is evaluated on all 1532 problems. Sampling and outcomes. Base A models generate up to 31,744 tokens and Base B models up to 3,072 tokens (the context limit of Qwen2.5-Math), with temperature 0.7 and top- p p 0.9; all outputs are graded by the same rule-based verifier. Because this reflects answer formatting rather than the problem, our main analysis on Base B uses the 249 problems on which at most a quarter of base samples lack a final answer; results on all 395 problems are reported in Appendix B . For every split of the runs into two equal halves we compute the Spearman correlation between the half means across problems and average, obtaining the split-half agreement r r ; with an odd number of runs we leave one run out of each split. The Spearman–Brown formula [ 26 , 2 ] extends r r to the reliability R R of the mean over all runs; intuitively, it answers how reliable the average of all runs is, given how well two halves of them agree. Under the classical model in which each run’s outcome is a shared component plus run-specific deviation, no a priori predictor can be expected to correlate with y ¯ p \bar{y}_{p} more than R \sqrt{R} , which we call the noise ceiling; the construction is standard in neuroscience [ 22 ] and has been used to bound per-item predictability for language models [ 38 ] . A practical recipe. To anticipate which held-out problems a new post-training run of a base model will improve, evaluate the base model and one existing checkpoint of it with a few dozen samples per problem, and rank problems by the checkpoint’s gain. No reference solutions, larger models or likelihood computations are needed, and the ranking is more informative than any a priori statistic we tested. For base models that are being post-trained for the first time, the noise ceiling shows how much room is left for a priori signals to grow into. 7 Related work Does post-training create new capabilities? Comparisons at large sampling budgets find that RLVR mostly sharpens capabilities the base model already has [ 35 ] , with analogous conclusions for on-policy distillation [ 27 , 14 ] ; others report expansion under prolonged training [ 17 ] , relate apparent limits to the composition of primitive skills [ 29 , 37 ] , or show that even spurious rewards improve Qwen2.5-Math [ 23 ] . We ask a different question: not whether the boundary moves in aggregate, but which problems move, and how predictable that is. Per-problem outcomes of RLVR. Yang et al. [32] show, for public RLVR pairs, that problems with the same base success rate can have different post-RL success rates and that these differences repeat across independent generation halves of the same pair. We ask a complementary question: whether different runs on the same base model agree with each other on which problems improve, how much of that agreement any signal could predict, and whether it carries over to a different base model. Chakma et al. [3] show that difficulty labels estimated from few rollouts are unstable, which motivates our many-sample design. Chen et al. [4] identify training problems that remain unlearnable and observe that correct-rollout likelihoods are similarly distributed for learnable and unlearnable groups. Zhou et al. [39] estimate a learnability prior for training problems from short probe training under one recipe. Our signals require no training, our outcomes are on held-out problems, and our ceiling is defined across recipes and groups. Selecting and allocating problems. Proposed signals include the student’s likelihood of verified solutions [ 30 ] , observed success counts [ 34 ] , internal circuit activations [ 5 ] and prefix recoverability [ 15 ] ; teacher-guided curricula [ 40 ] and strategy-conditioned exploration [ 6 ] target problems that are currently unsolvable. A recent controlled comparison finds no rollout-selection method that reliably beats uniform sampling [ 16 ] . Our measurements point to one reason: the closeness signals these methods build on capture only a minority of what post-training predictably changes. Reporting the noise ceiling alongside a signal’s correlation would make the remaining headroom explicit. 8 Conclusion Before post-training a model, can we tell which problems it will improve on? Across two base models and eighteen runs, the answer has three parts. What post-training fixes is shared across independent runs and specific to the base model. The closeness signals behind today’s data selection and curricula capture only a minority of it. And the outcomes of a single existing checkpoint capture more than any a priori signal, alone or combined. The noise ceiling turns the remaining gap into a number. We hope it becomes a routine companion to per-problem signals, and that closing the gap becomes a goal for the next generation of selection methods. References [1] Mislav Balunović et al.
